projects.title: E-Commerce Purchase-Prediction & Conversion Funnel Analysis

sectionHeadlines.summaryImpact: Why do some shoppers buy — and most just look?
sectionHeadlines.problemSpace: Conversion, not traffic, is the growth lever
sectionHeadlines.inputs: A full population log, not a sample
sectionHeadlines.discovery: Once carted, buyers almost always buy
sectionHeadlines.execution: Built to survive files that don't fit in memory

projects.cardDescription: Diagnosed why visitors leave without buying using 110M+ clickstream events from a real multi-category store — and found the leak is almost entirely upstream of checkout.
projects.impactStat: 0.92 ROC-AUC purchase model, holding at 0.946 a month later with no retraining
projects.oneSentenceDescription: A full-funnel behavioural diagnosis showing that once an item is carted it's bought 82.67% of the time — so the real leak, and the real opportunity, is at view → cart.
projects.summaryImpact:
Growing profit doesn't require more traffic — it's already there. The cheapest lever is converting shoppers who are already close to buying: the ones who've added something to cart. Across 42.4M October + 67.4M November 2019 clickstream events from a real multi-category online store — the full REES46 Marketing Platform dataset on Kaggle, not a sample — I diagnosed why visitors leave without buying, and where product, CX, and marketing teams can intervene.

The data says this is a **discovery problem, not a checkout problem:** at the event level, a cart converts to a purchase 82.67% of the time — yet 49.1% of October's cart-containing sessions still end with no purchase at all, since one session can cart repeatedly before converting once, or never. Either way, the leak is almost entirely upstream, at view → cart.

The core deliverable: a LightGBM model that scores which abandoned carts are closest to converting, so Marketing knows which sessions are worth a retargeting nudge — not just which customers converted historically.

Method: chunked pandas EDA on files too large for memory, session-level feature engineering across 9.2M October sessions, a LightGBM purchase-prediction model with SHAP, K-Means/decision-tree customer segmentation, and out-of-time validation on November.

summaryMetrics.label: of purchases from phones (27% of traffic)

projects.problemSpace:
Re-acquiring a new visitor costs money — a shopper who's already added something to cart has done most of the work of becoming a customer. Instead of treating every abandoned cart equally, retargeting budget should go to the shoppers behaviourally closest to the store's actual purchasers. View volume is already enormous — **96% of all events are views** — so the business doesn't need more traffic at this stage of the funnel; **it needs more of the traffic it already has to convert.** That reframes this from a marketing-acquisition problem into a full-funnel behavioural diagnosis.

Scope: two full months of clickstream — October and November 2019, chosen so Black Friday's seasonal noise can be separated from durable behaviour — **tracked down to the individual event:** every view, cart add, and purchase, with its category, brand, price, and timestamp. Five questions structure the story: which dimension (category, brand, price, time-of-day, day-of-week) most separates cart events from purchase events; can a cart event be scored by how "purchase-like" its context is; is there a point where that score becomes statistically indistinguishable from an actual purchase; does the pattern hold across both months; and which specific combinations should Marketing and CX prioritize first?

The output is **a rankable purchase-likeness score for any cart event** — directly usable by a retargeting system — with an honest account of exactly how far context alone can go, and where it runs out. Every finding below is tied to a named owner and a concrete action, not left as a standalone statistic.

stakeholders.description: Owns the cart/checkout experience — needs to know whether context alone is enough to act on, or whether richer session signals are required.
Owns on-site friction — needs to know which browsing contexts signal a shopper who's almost there versus one who was never going to convert.
Owns retargeting campaigns and remarketing spend — needs to know who to target and when.

inputs.description:
**eCommerce behavior data from multi-category store** — the REES46 Marketing Platform dataset on Kaggle. No secondary sources: every feature comes from two full CSV files, aggregated per `user_session` — **2019-Oct.csv** (5.6GB, 42.4M rows) and **2019-Nov.csv** (9GB, 67.4M rows).

Columns used: `event_time, event_type, user_id, product_id, brand, price, category_code, user_session`.

dataQuality.label: Data quality — reported transparently
items: 0.07% exact duplicate events removed.
`category_code` missing on 31.8% of rows, `brand` missing on 14.4% — both optional upstream catalog fields, not defects.
`product_id` is not a fully stable key: 0.11% of products showed more than one brand (SKU reuse), so brand-level joins can't assume 1:1.

Nulls are kept as null, never dropped or imputed — each category/brand-level aggregate excludes null rows for that specific field only, not the whole row, so a session's other fields aren't silently thrown away.

closingNote.label: Target & Key Predictors
items: **Target:** `purchased` — session-level binary, derived from `event_type` (1 if any event in the session was a purchase, 0 otherwise), not a raw column.
**Top predictors:** cart count, session duration, view count, n_unique_brands — all engineered per session, not per raw row.

categoryLeader.label: Category Leader
categoryLeader.heading: electronics.smartphone
categoryLeader.description: Samsung + Apple + Xiaomi make up ~50% of all purchases. Volume and efficiency leader at once.

priceBehaviour.label: Price Behaviour
priceBehaviour.description: A mild but consistent price-sensitivity signal right before checkout. Price is heavily right-skewed (electronics push the top end) — roughly 8-9% of sampled rows fall outside the IQR fence in both months. No negative prices; a small number of exact-$0 rows exist, likely free promotional items.

surprisingPatterns.label: Surprising Patterns
items: Average-priced items convert better than cheap or expensive ones — not the "cheaper converts better" pattern naive intuition would predict.

hypothesisVsReality.label: Hypothesis vs. Reality
items: Expected `category_code` to be the strongest signal, with price acting mostly as a secondary, category-specific modifier.

Instead: `category_code` is missing on ~32% of rows — too incomplete to rely on alone — and both price and timing carried meaningful independent signal. Timing mattered more than expected: a genuine update, not a confirmation.

deadEnds.label: Dead Ends
items: Chunked **reading** that still crashed the kernel: the first loader re-concatenated every chunk into one full DataFrame, so by the end the entire file was in memory anyway — invisible on a small sample, but it exhausted memory on the real 42M/67M-row files. Fixed by computing every EDA statistic as a running accumulator during the streaming pass itself, so the full table is never materialized.

A random row sample can't validate session-level cart-vs-purchase comparisons — a session's cart and purchase events are unlikely to both survive the same random draw. Fixed with a full-population lookup of which sessions ever converted, built incrementally across every chunk, so a sampled cart event can still be checked against its own session's true outcome.

secondaryModel.label: A Second Model — And a Real Correction
items: A separate binary model powers the cart-scoring output promised in Problem Space: `purchase` vs. `cart`, at the individual **event** level, using category, brand, price, and timing instead of session behaviour. Its segment-prioritization step (Q5) clusters with K-Prototypes rather than K-Means, since it needs to group on a mix of categorical (category, brand) and numeric (price, hour) features directly.

The first version also included `view` events, and `brand` came out as the #1 predictor. Removing `view` changed the answer entirely — `price` jumped to #1, `brand` dropped to #4. `view` is ~95% of the data, so that version was really learning "what makes someone engage at all," not "what makes an already-engaged shopper buy instead of just cart" — the actual question. A correction to the framing, not just the model.

executionDeadEnds.label: Dead Ends
items: Tested per-session `n_unique_products` as a feature — dropped it: ~200k distinct values made it the most expensive feature to compute, for little added signal over view count and `n_unique_categories`.
Rejected the "best" clustering result (k=2, highest silhouette score) — it was just a trivial one-time-vs-repeat-visitor split with no business use.

methodology.heading: Engineering constraint
methodology.description: 42.4M/67.4M-row files processed in **2M-row chunks with incremental aggregation**. Session-level grouping (9.2M sessions) took ~27 min/month — `user_session` has near-UUID cardinality, unlike low-cardinality hour/brand/category aggregates.

methodology.heading: Model choice
methodology.description: **LightGBM binary classifier**, `is_unbalance=True` for the 6.8% positive rate, early stopping on validation AUC. Chosen over logistic regression, since features interact non-linearly and LightGBM handles day-of-week natively, and over Random Forest — LightGBM's leaf-wise, histogram-based growth trains faster at this row count, and boosting corrects earlier errors iteratively, where Random Forest's bagged trees can't.

methodology.heading: Leakage discipline
methodology.description: Excluded `user_session`/`user_id`, the literal purchase count, and `n_events` (which encodes purchase count indirectly).

methodology.heading: Evaluation trap avoided
methodology.description: `predict_proba ≥ 0.5` classifies everything as "no purchase" — **93%-accurate, useless.** Picked an F1-optimal threshold from the precision-recall curve instead; report ROC-AUC/PR-AUC as the primary metrics.

methodology.heading: Segmentation
methodology.description: K-Means (k=6, chosen by silhouette among k=3–7) plus a shallow decision tree as a human-readable cross-check — both trained on behavioural features only, **purchase outcome held out entirely.**

methodology.heading: Validation
methodology.description: Scored the Oct-trained model on unseen Nov sessions with the exact same fixed threshold — a direct test of whether Oct alone was enough to build on, without retraining. In production, the same approach extends to ongoing monitoring: score each week's fresh sessions against the same fixed threshold, track ROC-AUC and the purchase-rate base rate over time — the same comparison that surfaced the Oct→Nov swing — and **treat a sustained AUC drop or base-rate shift as the retrain trigger**, rather than retraining on a fixed schedule.

items.text: **More page views** push toward purchase.
**Browsing more distinct brands** pushes away from purchase — comparison shopping predicts against conversion.
A **higher max price viewed** pushes slightly away from purchase.

keyResults.label: Key Results
items: Once a shopper carts, **50.9%** of October's cart-containing sessions went on to purchase — the flip side of the 49.1% that didn't.
Purchase rate dropped from **6.81% in October to 5.61% in November** — a swing worth planning around, not dismissing as noise.

projects.businessInterpretation:
In plain terms: this model is good at spotting a shopper who's already engaged — long session, multiple items carted — but not yet good at explaining which specific thing (a category, a brand, a time of day) would have changed a browser's mind.

The segment and category findings above are a strong "where to look first" — not yet a proven "what to change." Treat them as a prioritized shortlist for testing, not a finished playbook.

This held up under multiple checks, not just one run: removing key features (the ablation study), testing across a range of cluster counts, and re-scoring on an entirely unseen month.

items.text: Reduce brand-comparison friction — clearer comparison tools, stronger recommendation ranking. Comparison-shoppers convert worse than focused browsers.
Retarget the "long single-visit browser" segment — 946k users, ~57 min average session, only 13.2% convert. An already-warm audience that just doesn't return.
Invest in discovery/recommendation surfaces, not checkout UX. Cart→purchase is already 82.67% — checkout has a low ceiling. View→cart has the highest possible upside.

Treat the Oct→Nov purchase-rate swing (6.81% → 5.61%) as a recurring planning input — a promotional month converts differently than a typical one, so forecasts and targets should account for it, not treat it as one-off noise.

limitations: `category_code`/`brand` missingness (31.8%/14.4%) and `product_id`'s unreliable brand key
No demographic or cross-session purchase-history data — everything is within-session only
Segment/category rankings are relative signals, not calibrated probabilities
Only two months tested (Oct–Nov) — seasonal patterns beyond that aren't covered
nextSteps: A/B test the brand-comparison-friction hypothesis
Build the live monitoring dashboard as a separate deliverable
Extend the model with a Nov-trained or combined Oct+Nov version if drift widens
Extend the feature set with cross-session purchase history, if it becomes available — the largest untested lever

projects.title: Advertising Revenue & Sales Efficiency Growth Diagnostic

sectionHeadlines.summaryImpact: From a $3.60M revenue gap to the accounts that need action
sectionHeadlines.problemSpace: Revenue alone cannot explain why commercial performance changes
sectionHeadlines.inputs: One governed model connecting advertising and sales operations
sectionHeadlines.execution: Built as a traceable decision system, not a collection of charts
sectionHeadlines.results: Every portfolio signal ends in a specific commercial action

projects.cardDescription: Built a five-page Power BI decision system that connects advertising performance, advertiser lifecycle, sales activity, pipeline and targets to diagnose revenue and prioritise 720 accounts.
projects.impactStat: $10.50M revenue vs. $14.10M target, diagnosed through campaign, lifecycle and sales evidence
projects.oneSentenceDescription: An end-to-end commercial analytics system that explains why advertising revenue is below target and converts campaign, lifecycle and sales evidence into transparent account actions.
projects.summaryImpact:
The executive view showed **$10.50M in advertising revenue against a $14.10M target** — a **$3.60M adverse variance, or 25.5% below target**. The challenge was not displaying that gap; it was making it diagnosable. Revenue could move because of campaign efficiency, advertiser acquisition and churn, account spending, sales coverage or pipeline conversion.

I built a five-page Power BI decision system that moves from executive monitoring to campaign diagnosis, sales-team efficiency and a prioritised account worklist. An Advertiser 360 drill-through page exposes the campaign, opportunity and contact evidence behind each recommendation.

The portfolio contained **720 fictional advertisers** and used transparent Rescue, Reactivate, Optimise, Upsell, Onboard and Maintain rules. This makes every recommendation explainable in an interview and auditable by a business user instead of hiding it inside a black-box score.
projects.problemSpace:
A fictional global advertising platform had performance data but no unified view connecting advertising revenue, campaign outcomes, advertiser lifecycle, sales activities, opportunity pipeline and commercial targets. Leadership could see whether revenue moved, but not isolate the combination of campaign, portfolio and execution factors behind the movement.

The central question was: **Why is advertising revenue above or below target, which advertiser segments contain the strongest growth opportunities, and how should the sales team prioritise its effort?** The report therefore had to support three different decision levels without producing contradictory metrics: leadership monitoring, manager-level diagnosis and account-level action.

The design deliberately separates **platform advertising revenue** — advertiser spend paid to the fictional platform — from **attributed advertiser revenue**, the advertiser's sales outcome. Confusing these two concepts would make revenue and ROAS analysis commercially misleading.

stakeholders.description: Needs revenue, target and advertiser-growth diagnosis to set commercial priorities.
Needs capacity, contact coverage and pipeline evidence to rebalance portfolios and improve execution.
Needs an ordered worklist explaining which advertiser to contact and why.
Needs funnel and efficiency comparisons across platform, objective and market segments.

inputs.description:
A public synthetic digital-marketing dataset supplied **30,000 advertising-performance records and 35 source fields** covering 2023–2025. Because it did not contain the commercial entities required for sales-efficiency analysis, I generated a documented supplementary layer for advertisers, representatives, opportunities, activities, targets and calendar-month lifecycle status.

The governed model contains conformed Date, Advertiser, Sales Representative, Platform, Geography and Advertising Entity dimensions connected to advertising-performance, advertiser-month, opportunity, sales-activity and target facts.

dataQuality.label: Governance and reconciliation
items: Preserved all 30,000 original performance records and documented the source grain and date-format mismatch.
Reconciled $12,636,409.06 platform advertising revenue, 1,701,763,447 impressions, 25,617,140 clicks and 322,798 conversions across source, SQL and Power BI.
Validated grains, foreign keys, lifecycle exclusivity, opportunity probabilities and impossible funnel relationships.
Used safe division for CTR, CVR, CPA, CPC, ROAS, retention, win rate and target attainment.

closingNote.label: Synthetic-data disclosure
items: All advertisers, representatives, opportunities, activities and targets are fictional and generated reproducibly.
Findings demonstrate analytical method and must not be interpreted as evidence about TikTok or another real advertising platform.

hypothesisVsReality.label: Hypothesis vs. Reality
items: Expected weak revenue to be explained mainly by campaign efficiency. The completed model showed that the same revenue result can require different actions depending on lifecycle, ROAS, contact coverage, pipeline and unused account potential.

A simple sales leaderboard looked attractive initially, but it confounded portfolio size with performance. I replaced it with capacity, process and coverage exceptions so managers could diagnose systems rather than rank people simplistically.

deadEnds.label: Analytical boundaries
items: Most source campaign and advertisement identifiers appear only once, so I rejected continuous campaign-level trend claims and kept time analysis at governed portfolio and advertiser grains.

The seven original account labels were broad archetypes, not a sufficient advertiser population. They were retained as archetypes while a separate fictional advertiser dimension was generated for account analysis.

methodology.heading: SQL architecture
methodology.description: Built raw, staging, dimensional, fact and business-view layers in **Microsoft SQL Server**, using CTEs, window functions, constraints and reconciliation queries. Chosen over **PostgreSQL**, which would do the same modelling job at no licence cost, because the deliverable here is an end-to-end Microsoft BI chain (SQL Server → Power Query → semantic model → DAX) — the stack the BI Developer roles this targets actually run — and routing Power BI to Postgres over ODBC would add a hop without demonstrating anything extra. Chosen over a cloud warehouse (**BigQuery** or **Snowflake**) because at this volume there is nothing to distribute: 720 advertisers and 2,400 opportunities sit comfortably in a single instance, so distributed compute would add cost and query latency in exchange for headroom the project never uses.

methodology.heading: Synthetic commercial layer
methodology.description: Used **Python** and documented configuration to generate 720 advertisers, 24 representatives, 2,400 opportunities, sales activities and monthly targets.

methodology.heading: Semantic model
methodology.description: Connected five fact tables through conformed dimensions with one-to-many relationships, controlled filter direction and explicit date-role handling.

methodology.heading: DAX governance
methodology.description: Created safe, context-aware measures for revenue, target variance, funnel conversion, lifecycle, pipeline, coverage, capacity and advertiser prioritisation.

methodology.heading: Action logic
methodology.description: Implemented interpretable **Rescue, Reactivate, Optimise, Upsell, Onboard and Maintain** rules with a reason and priority order for every account. Chosen over a **trained propensity model** (churn or upsell likelihood scored per account) for two reasons. First, the commercial layer is synthetic: a classifier fitted to it would be recovering the generator's own rules, which is circular and would prove nothing about real advertiser behaviour. Second, the consumer is a sales manager who has to defend the call to the rep working the account — "flagged Rescue because spend fell quarter-on-quarter while rep activity fell with it" is auditable and arguable; "0.78 propensity" is neither. The trade-off is real: fixed rules don't adapt, their thresholds need manual tuning, and they will miss edge cases a model trained on genuine outcome labels would catch.

methodology.heading: Report experience
methodology.description: Designed four diagnostic pages plus **Advertiser 360 drill-through**, connecting executive performance to the evidence behind an account action.

keyResults.label: Key Results
items: The selected executive view identified a **$3.60M revenue shortfall**, 25.5% below its $14.10M target.
The governed source reconciled to **1.70B impressions, 25.62M clicks and 322,798 conversions**.
The Action Centre translated portfolio evidence into an ordered worklist across **720 advertisers**, with account-level drill-through for validation.
The final report joins leadership, campaign, sales-manager and account-executive decisions without changing KPI definitions between pages.

projects.businessInterpretation:

items.text: Prioritise account interventions by lifecycle, revenue momentum, ROAS and unused potential rather than revenue size alone.

Calibrate recommendation thresholds with commercial stakeholders and track accepted actions and realised outcomes before treating the rules as production policy.

sectionHeadlines.problemSpace: A churn score isn't a spending plan
sectionHeadlines.inputs: 21.5 million real transactions, not a sample

sectionHeadlines.results: Risk crossed with real spend, not a proxy

projects.cardDescription: Diagnosed which real music-streaming subscribers are worth a retention offer using 21.5M real transactions from KKBox (WSDM Cup 2018) — crossing churn risk against actual subscription spend, and catching three real methodology bugs before trusting any result.
projects.impactStat: 84.2% of real cancellations caught at the deployed threshold — risk crossed with actual subscription spend, not a proxy
projects.oneSentenceDescription: A subscriber-level churn risk score crossed with real subscription spend — built on 21.5M real KKBox transactions, with three real methodology bugs caught and fixed before any result was trusted.
projects.targetIndustryRole: Subscription Media Retention, Lifecycle Marketing & Data Science
projects.summaryImpact:
A churn score tells a retention team who's about to cancel. It doesn't tell them who's worth spending a retention budget on. Built on **21,547,746 real transactions** from KKBox, a real Asian music-streaming subscription service (the WSDM Cup 2018 Churn Prediction Challenge on Kaggle) — not a synthetic or engagement-proxy dataset — I built a subscriber-level churn risk model and crossed it against real subscription spend to produce a spendable priority order for retention budget.

The data says the churn definition itself has to be earned, not assumed: **96.8% of all renewals that happen, happen within 30 days of expiry** — the point this data's own renewal-gap curve flattens, and the threshold this project's churn label is built on, not copied from a blog post.

The core deliverable: a risk-value quadrant that separates subscribers worth an active retention push from subscribers who are at risk but not worth the cost of saving — so a retention team spends a $75 offer where it returns, not on whoever looks about to leave.

Method: chunked pandas processing across 21.5M+ transaction rows, out-of-time validation (never a random split), a LightGBM churn model with SHAP, K-Means subscriber segmentation, and three real methodology bugs — caught and fixed, not hidden — documented in full below.

summaryMetrics.label: of cancellations caught at the deployed threshold
real methodology bugs caught before shipping

projects.problemSpace:
Retention budget usually gets spent reactively — on whoever looks about to cancel, regardless of whether they were ever paying much. **Re-acquiring a cancelled subscriber costs money; a subscriber who's already paying has already done the hard part.** Instead of treating every at-risk subscriber the same, retention spend should go to subscribers who are both behaviourally close to cancelling and worth the cost of keeping.

Scope: 21.5 million real transactions from KKBox, a real music-streaming subscription service, spanning January 2015 through February 2017 — tracked down to the individual transaction, with plan price, amount actually paid, auto-renew status, and cancellation flag. The churn threshold (30 days of no renewal after expiry) was derived from this data's own renewal-gap distribution, not assumed, and matches the official WSDM competition rule for an independent reason, not by copying it.

The output is **a rankable churn-risk score for every subscriber, crossed against real subscription spend** — directly usable for retention-offer prioritisation — with an honest account of where a simpler logistic-regression baseline actually beats the deployed LightGBM model, and where three real methodology bugs had to be caught and fixed before any number could be trusted.

stakeholders.description: Owns retention-offer spend — needs to know which subscribers are both at risk and worth the cost of an offer.
Owns the retention budget — needs the cost/return economics stated explicitly, not buried inside a black-box score.
Owns the model and its validation discipline — needs the leakage tests and out-of-time validation a real production deployment would require.

inputs.description:
**Real subscription transaction data from a real music-streaming service** — the KKBox Churn Prediction Challenge (WSDM Cup 2018) on Kaggle. Every feature comes from **transactions.csv** (21,547,746 rows, Jan 2015–Feb 2017) joined against **members_v3.csv** (6,769,473 members) on member ID.

Columns used: `msno, transaction_date, membership_expire_date, payment_plan_days, plan_list_price, actual_amount_paid, is_auto_renew, is_cancel, registration_init_time, registered_via`.

dataQuality.label: Data quality — reported transparently
items: 12.3% of transaction rows had no matching member record — dropped from member-joined analysis, an explicit decision, not silent.
153 transactions predated the member's own registration date (69 members affected) — dropped.
2.52% of rows were same-day repeat transactions — a billing-correction pattern, not real cadence — deduplicated to the last transaction of the day for recency/frequency features.

0.71% of rows showed a membership expiry before the transaction that created it — 95.8% of those turned out to be legitimate immediate-cancellation records; only the remaining ~6,450 non-cancel-linked rows were treated as genuine anomalies and dropped.

closingNote.label: Target & Key Predictors
items: **Target:** `is_churn` — derived independently from this data's own 30-day renewal-gap rule, not imported from the competition's own supplied label, which measures a narrower, differently-defined population.
**Top predictor:** `days_since_cutoff` (reference date minus scoring cutoff) — by a wide margin (mean |SHAP| = 3.72). `days_since_last_transaction` and `is_auto_renew` follow.

surprisingPatterns.label: Surprising Patterns
items: Logistic regression (ROC-AUC 0.936, PR-AUC 0.925) beats the deployed LightGBM (ROC-AUC 0.676, PR-AUC 0.647) on every headline metric — reported honestly rather than favouring the "primary" model, since `days_since_cutoff`'s dominance is close to linear and LightGBM's added flexibility wasn't needed for a leak-free, well-specified feature set.

hypothesisVsReality.label: Hypothesis vs. Reality
items: Expected the churn threshold to simply match the WSDM competition's own published rule (30 days) as a given, with feature engineering as the real work.

Instead: the 30-day threshold had to be earned independently from this data's own renewal-gap curve (96.8% of renewals happen within it) before it could be trusted — it happened to match the official rule, but for a reason grounded in this data, not because the rule was copied. And feature engineering turned out to hide a genuinely missing signal (`days_since_cutoff`) that was more consequential than any of the originally-planned feature families.

deadEnds.label: Dead Ends
items: The original dataset candidate — a 1M-player mobile gaming login/spend log — looked real and event-level, until the gap-distribution check showed every one of 8.6M consecutive-login gaps falling inside a suspiciously exact [1.0, 7.04]-day bounded random walk, and `reg_ts` exactly equalling the first `auth_ts` for all 1,000,000 users with zero variance. Neither is something a real registration/login system produces. Dropped and re-sourced entirely — the project's whole domain pivoted from gaming to subscription media as a result.

The competition's own supplied `is_churn` label (9.0% churn rate) looked like a ready-made target — kept only as a reference check, not the source of truth, since it snapshots just currently-active subscribers at one fixed point, not the full population with sufficient history that this project's own churn definition evaluates.

executionDeadEnds.label: Three Real Bugs — Caught Before Shipping
items: **Cutoff-date-as-churn-proxy leak.** The first design picked each member's own last eligible transaction as their one labeled row and split train/validation by that date — on real data this produced 69% churn in train vs 7% in validation from the same population, because a churned member's history simply stops early while an active member's keeps getting pushed later. Fixed by evaluating every member as of a shared external reference date per split, guaranteeing disjoint membership by construction.

**A missing recency feature, not leakage.** A tuned LightGBM showed near-perfect PR-AUC (~0.97–0.99) on an internal split of train but collapsed to PR-AUC=0.54 on real validation — worse than the untuned model. Traced to a genuinely missing feature: `days_since_last_transaction` measured the gap between two of a member's own past transactions, but never the gap to the actual scoring/reference date — the single most fundamental recency signal in churn modeling. Fixed by adding `days_since_cutoff` directly — fully known at scoring time, not leaky — which became the dominant SHAP feature by a wide margin.

**A population-composition split wearing a time split's clothes.** Guaranteeing member-disjointness by excluding anyone already used in train silently restricted validation to only newer, shorter-tenured members, since any long-tenured member was always claimed by train first. This broke LightGBM catastrophically (ROC-AUC fell below 0.5, worse than random) while logistic regression partially masked it through feature scaling — which is what exposed the gap between the two models and triggered the investigation. Fixed by partitioning members into random disjoint pools before any time-based eligibility logic runs, confirmed by matching tenure distributions across splits (train median 893 days, validation median 898).

methodology.heading: Engineering constraint
methodology.description: 21.5M-row transaction file processed in chunks. Member-level features are built from full transaction history per member, not a fixed rolling window, since Phase 3 eligibility excludes anyone without prior transaction history rather than truncating it.

methodology.heading: Model choice
methodology.description: **LightGBM** (n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05, num_leaves=31, is_unbalance=True) as the deployed model, matching the e-commerce project's stack — chosen despite logistic regression scoring higher on real validation, since a hyperparameter-tuning attempt didn't beat this simple config, and the untuned config was already the stronger candidate on generalization, not internal-split performance.

methodology.heading: Leakage discipline
methodology.description: 4 automated tests (`test_no_future_events`, `test_label_from_prediction_window_only`, `test_no_member_overlap`, `test_feature_nulls`) run on every build — the 3 bugs below were all caught by a metric looking *too good*, not by a red test, which is the harder failure mode to catch.

methodology.heading: Validation
methodology.description: **Out-of-time validation** — train cutoff 2016-06-30, validation cutoff 2017-01-29 (the latest date a labeled expiry can still resolve within the data) — never a random split, since a random split on time-series subscription data flatters the model and hides exactly the kind of population-composition bug found in Bug 3.

methodology.heading: Segmentation
methodology.description: K-Means (k=3, chosen by elbow + silhouette among k=2–8) on behavioural features only — recency, frequency, monetisation, tenure, trajectory — **never on `is_churn` or the predicted risk score**, which would make a "high-risk segment" a tautology rather than a finding.

items.text: **Days since the scoring cutoff** (`days_since_cutoff`) dominates by a wide margin (mean |SHAP| = 3.72) — non-churned members' last transaction sits a median 14 days before the reference date; churned members' sits a median 151 days before it.
**Longer gap since the last transaction** pushes toward churn — the classic recency signal, though weaker than expected once `days_since_cutoff` had its own feature.

**Auto-renew enabled** pushes toward staying — the plain-language dashboard explanation for this had to be fixed to branch on the actual SHAP sign, not the raw feature value, after an early version occasionally produced reassuring-sounding text on a risk-increasing case.

keyResults.label: Key Results
items: LightGBM catches **84.2%** of real cancellations at the deployed threshold, at 45.9% precision — a deliberately wide net, the correct consequence of a cheap $75 offer against a $894 assumed retained-subscriber value, not a bug.

Logistic regression outperforms the deployed LightGBM on every headline metric (ROC-AUC 0.936 vs 0.676, PR-AUC 0.925 vs 0.647) — reported as the honest finding it is, not softened because LightGBM was the "planned" model.

projects.businessInterpretation:
In plain terms: this model is good at knowing *when* a subscriber is likely to leave — `days_since_cutoff` alone carries most of the signal — but the honest finding is that a simpler, more transparent logistic regression predicts it just as well, if not better, once the real recency signal is present as its own feature.

The risk-value quadrant is a strong "where to spend retention budget first," not a proven "this offer will work" — the $75/$894/30% economics behind it are explicitly assumed, not observed, and are stated as such everywhere they're used.

This held up under real scrutiny, not just one run: two of the three bugs above were caught precisely because a result looked *too good* rather than because a test failed red, and the final numbers survived out-of-time validation on a genuinely later, unseen period.

items.text: Spend the $75 retention offer on the Priority Save quadrant first (44.8% of subscribers, 47.6% churn, high value) — then Low-Cost Nudge (28.0%, 43.1% churn) — before Quiet Value — Monitor, which is lower-risk by the deployed threshold but still sits at 39.6% churn and should not be treated as safe.

Model the $75-offer / $894-value / 30%-success economics explicitly in the retention budget, and revisit all three assumed numbers against real offer-redemption data once a pilot runs — the quadrant sizes are real, the dollar assumptions underneath them are not yet.

Deploy logistic regression, not LightGBM, if interpretability and the stronger real validation numbers matter more than the flexibility LightGBM offers — this project's own data doesn't reward that flexibility.

Treat the three bugs documented here as the differentiator they are, not a footnote — a model whose builder can show real bugs found and fixed is more trustworthy than one presented as clean on the first attempt.

limitations: Retention-offer cost ($75), retained-subscriber value ($894), and offer success rate (30%) are all explicitly assumed, not observed from real offer-redemption data.
`user_logs_v2.csv` (March 2017 listening activity) was scoped out of the backtested model entirely — live-scoring-only enrichment, never validated against real outcomes.

Real validation churn rates (30.6%–41.2%) run well above the competition's own reference label (9.0%) for a documented reason (a different population definition) — but this makes the two numbers easy to misread as inconsistent if that reason isn't carried forward.
Segments and quadrants are relative risk/value groupings, not calibrated probabilities of an individual subscriber's outcome.
nextSteps: Pilot the $75 offer against the Priority Save quadrant and replace the assumed 30% success rate with a real measured one
Enable GitHub Pages / publish the dashboard for live sharing, and wire up a real repeat-scoring cadence
Extend the feature set with `user_logs_v2.csv` listening-intensity signals once a full year of logs, not one month, is available
Re-run the risk-value quadrant with real offer-redemption data in place of the assumed economics

projects.oneSentenceDescription: A dbt-core + DuckDB pipeline that ingests openly synthetic, deliberately corrupted ad-creative performance data and proves it can still deliver reliable same-day numbers — the deliverable is the pipeline, not an advertising finding.
projects.targetIndustryRole: BI Developer, Data Engineer, Analytics Engineer (marketing-adjacent)
projects.summaryImpact:
Media buyers usually find out which creatives are winning a week after the numbers mattered. **The deliverable here is the pipeline, not the analysis** — real creative-level ad performance data isn't published anywhere (even the Facebook Ad Library exposes creative content, not performance), so this project uses openly synthetic data with deliberately realistic failure modes instead of pretending a scraped dataset is something it isn't.

Built with dbt-core and DuckDB: a generator injects **8 named defect types** into 96 daily drop files — late arrivals, restated numbers, exact and near duplicates, a schema change mid-stream, nulled fields, a clicks-exceed-impressions platform bug, and one day the platform never delivers at all — logged to a ground-truth manifest so every defect's handling can be checked against a known answer, not eyeballed.

The pipeline reconciles to that ground truth exactly, with one real distinction worth explaining rather than hiding: **three of the eight defect types are never corrected by the upstream platform**, so a pipeline that "fixed" them would be inventing numbers. The other five — including a missing day that turned out to also swallow nearby late-arriving rows — resolve correctly through a 7-day lookback window and a stated latest-delivery-wins dedup rule.

CI runs the full daily cycle end to end (generate → load → `dbt build` + 10 tests → publish), with a public lineage graph and a thin dashboard, both hosted and live, not local-only.

projects.problemSpace:
Same-day creative performance is a genuine pain point in paid social — buying teams typically wait a week for platform reporting to stabilise, by which point a losing creative has already burned budget. The honest version of that pitch: what's actually being demonstrated here is **pipeline engineering** — transforms, tests, incremental loading, graceful failure — the skills a BI Developer or Data Engineer interview actually probes, not an advertising insight. A pipeline's quality is proven by how it handles hostile input, and generating that hostile input on purpose is standard practice in how real data teams test their own pipelines.

Scope: a **dbt-core + DuckDB** pipeline (swapped in for an originally-scoped dbt + BigQuery stack for zero cloud cost with no loss of demonstrated skill — dbt models are close to portable, and knowing why is itself interview material), orchestrated by GitHub Actions, with a hostile-input generator standing in for the ad platform. What's **not** claimed: any advertising finding. No "lifting CTR 18%." The CTR/CPC/CPA numbers in this pipeline are plumbing-test water.

stakeholders.description: Consumes the pipeline's output — needs to know which numbers are final and which are still provisional, without having to ask.
Owns the lookback window, dedup rule, and test suite — needs each one stated and reasoned, not defaulted.
Would consume the top-decile flagging in a real deployment — needs to trust that a flagged creative actually cleared a meaningful volume floor, not a lucky handful of impressions.

inputs.description: Openly synthetic, generated by a seeded Python script (`src/generator.py`), not scraped or sampled from any real platform — stated plainly because real creative-level ad performance data is proprietary and isn't published anywhere. 484 creatives across 25 campaigns over a 95-day window, with realistic daily performance (log-normal impressions, Beta-distributed CTR/CVR per creative, day-of-week seasonality) as the ground truth, then corrupted on delivery.

stats.label: daily drop files, each independently corrupted
individual defect events logged to the manifest

dataQuality.label: Defect types — reported transparently, not smoothed over
items: 2,656 late-arriving rows, delivered 1–3 days after their event date.
1,260 restated rows — an initial wrong value followed by a corrected one 1–2 days later.
109 exact duplicates and 111 near-duplicates (same key, a jittered impressions value) delivered within a single file.
276 nulled fields and 78 rows where clicks exceed impressions — a real platform bug pattern — both left uncorrected on purpose, since the generator never issues a fix for either.
1 schema-drift event (`spend` renamed to `cost`, a new `video_completion_rate` column added) and 1 day the platform never delivers at all.

closingNote.label: Dedup rule & lookback window
items: **Dedup rule:** latest delivery wins, tie-broken deterministically by position within a file when two rows share a key inside the same drop — a stated, defendable choice, not an unexamined assumption.
**Lookback window: 7 days** — covers the generator's worst case (a 3-day late arrival, plus a restatement correction up to 2 more days on top of that = 5 days) with a 2-day margin.

surprisingPatterns.label: Surprising Pattern
items: A platform outage doesn't just cost the missing day. Of the 281 rows the pipeline couldn't reconcile back to ground truth, 253 were on the missing day itself — but 28 more were late-arriving rows from the three days *before* it that happened to be scheduled for delivery on that exact date, and vanished with it.

hypothesisVsReality.label: Hypothesis vs. Reality
items: Expected the reconciliation test to simply confirm the pipeline matches ground truth once dedup and the lookback window were in place.

Instead: the first version failed for a real reason, not a bug in the test — it expected three defect types (nulled fields, the clicks-exceed-impressions bug, and same-file near-duplicates) to match ground truth, which isn't possible without inventing numbers, since the generator never issues a correction for any of the three. Fixed by scoping the comparison to defects that genuinely do resolve, and by adding a `had_same_drop_duplicate` column so the near-duplicate ambiguity is visible in the data rather than silently resolved.

deadEnds.label: Dead Ends
items: Considered adding a ninth defect type — a partial or paginated API pull returning fewer campaigns than expected — but rejected it as a row-level variant of the missing-day defect rather than a genuinely new failure mode, to avoid scope creep beyond the spec's own defect list.

executionDeadEnds.label: Three Real Bugs — Caught Before Shipping
items: **An untracked empty directory silently broke the first real CI run.** `dbt/seeds/` only ever contained a gitignored CSV, and git doesn't track empty directories — so a fresh checkout had no `dbt/seeds/` at all, and the workflow's plain `cp` step into it failed outright, skipping `dbt seed` and `dbt build` entirely. Local testing never caught it, because the directory already existed locally from earlier manual runs. Fixed with a tracked `.gitkeep` placeholder plus a defensive `mkdir -p`.

**A settings-page click that looked like it worked, didn't.** Enabling GitHub Pages (Settings → Pages → Source: GitHub Actions) is a repo-settings change outside the build agent's permission scope, so it had to be done by hand — and the first attempt silently didn't save, with no indication from the GitHub web UI that anything was wrong. Caught by querying the GitHub API directly instead of trusting the settings page, twice, before the second attempt was confirmed to have actually taken.

**The results table broke on an actual mobile viewport, not in theory.** The thin dashboard's top-decile table overflowed the page instead of scrolling within itself at 375px width — caught by checking a real mobile viewport before shipping, not assumed fine because it looked fine on desktop. Fixed with a scoped `overflow-x: auto` wrapper.

methodology.heading: Stack
methodology.description: dbt-core + DuckDB, orchestrated by GitHub Actions — chosen over the originally-scoped dbt + BigQuery for zero cloud cost with no loss of demonstrated skill; dbt models are close to portable across warehouses, and knowing why is itself interview material.

methodology.heading: Raw layer contract
methodology.description: The loader lands every delivered row verbatim — duplicates and superseded restatements included — rather than cleaning on ingest. The raw layer's job is to preserve exactly what the platform delivered, which is what makes the ground-truth manifest checkable against it later; dedup is the staging layer's job, not the loader's.

methodology.heading: Dedup rule
methodology.description: Latest delivery wins. Within the same drop file, a deterministic tiebreak (row position) resolves duplicate/near-duplicate collisions — an arbitrary but reproducible choice, not a claim about which of two same-key rows is "truer," since the data itself doesn't say.

methodology.heading: Incremental strategy
methodology.description: `stg_creative_performance` reprocesses a 7-day lookback window on every run via `delete+insert`, rather than only ever appending — long enough to absorb the generator's worst-case corruption lag (5 days) with margin, short enough that reprocessing cost stays negligible on local DuckDB.

methodology.heading: Ranking metric
methodology.description: Top-decile flagging by CTR alone, chosen for simplicity over CPA or a blended score, restricted to creatives clearing a 1,000-daily-impression floor grounded in the data's own 10th percentile — so a handful of impressions can't "win" the ranking by accident.

methodology.heading: Test design
methodology.description: 10 dbt tests, one of them (`assert_clicks_lte_impressions`) configured `severity=warn` on purpose — it's supposed to find rows every run, since that defect is never corrected upstream, and treating an expected finding as a red CI failure would just train everyone to ignore it.

keyResults.label: Key Results
items: Reconciles to the ground truth exactly across the pipeline's lookback window, for every defect type the platform is actually capable of correcting (late arrival, restatement, cross-file duplicates).
All 10 dbt tests green except the one designed to warn — roughly 76–78 rows caught by `assert_clicks_lte_impressions` every run, exactly the defect it exists to surface.
CI runs the full daily cycle (generate → load → `dbt build` → publish) on push, PR, a daily schedule, and manual dispatch — not a one-off local demo.

projects.businessInterpretation:
In plain terms: this pipeline proves it can tell the difference between data that will get better on its own and data that won't. Late-arriving and restated numbers self-heal within a week without anyone doing anything; a clicks-exceed-impressions bug or a day the platform loses entirely does not, and the pipeline says so out loud — a defect log and a freshness indicator, not a silently-wrong dashboard.

That distinction is the actual deliverable. A BI lead reading this pipeline's output can trust the "latest finalized day" number completely, and knows exactly why the "latest available day" number might still move. The CTR/CPC/CPA figures themselves are not a finding about advertising — they're synthetic, and the README says so in its first paragraph.

items.text: Trust the "latest finalized day" number without caveats; treat anything inside the 7-day lookback window as provisional, and read the defect log before treating a day-over-day swing as a real signal rather than a still-resolving restatement.

The lookback window (7 days) and dedup rule (latest-delivery-wins) are both stated, reasoned choices, not defaults — see the repo's spec session log for the exact trade-off math before changing either.

The engineering depth is in what the pipeline refuses to paper over — three defect types stay visible on purpose, and the reconciliation test's own build history (a real failure, fixed for a real reason) is in the commit log, not smoothed over in this write-up.

limitations: Openly synthetic upstream by design — no real advertising platform's performance data is used or claimed; the CTR/CPC/CPA numbers are plumbing-test water, not an advertising finding.

Single-platform schema, invented for this project — a real Meta or Google Ads export changes three concrete things: the column set (Meta's Marketing API returns nested insight objects per ad, not a flat CSV — impressions/clicks/spend live under an “insights” edge keyed by date range, and creative metadata is a separate object joined by ad ID); the auth flow (OAuth2 with a refreshable long-lived token, not a filesystem drop — the loader's “pick up new files” model becomes “poll an API on a schedule and handle token expiry”); and rate limits (a rolling points-based budget per ad account, so a same-day pull for many accounts needs backoff and batching designed in from the start). None of this touches the staging/marts layer — dedup, lookback, and the metric definitions are platform-agnostic by construction — it only changes the loader.

DuckDB won't be the right engine forever, and knowing where it stops matters more than defending it as a permanent choice. DuckDB is single-node and in-process — no distributed query engine, no built-in multi-writer concurrency. In practice that's comfortable well into the tens of gigabytes on a single modern machine, which covers this project by a wide margin and would still comfortably cover a single mid-size advertiser's full creative-performance history. The real switch point isn't a row count — it's needing concurrent writers, compute larger than one machine can hold in memory, or serving many analysts' ad-hoc queries at once without one heavy query blocking another. BigQuery (or Snowflake) earns its cost at that point, not before it — and dbt models port across both with only the adapter and a handful of engine-specific functions changing.

Top-decile ranking rounds coarsely on small same-day campaign groups (fewer than ~10 creatives) — `percent_rank`'s granularity means the flagged share runs closer to 12–18% than an exact 10% for those groups.

projects.cardDescription: Tested whether complaint themes inside Steam reviews rise before a game's review score collapses. They don't — both events were triggered by dated developer announcements, so themes and score moved the same day. The useful finding is same-day diagnosis: the theme mix names the cause within hours.
projects.impactStat: A 12-point single-day drop rule fires 3 times in 9 months with zero false alarms; the obvious level rule fires 35 times, 29 of them nothing
projects.oneSentenceDescription: 886,850 Steam reviews across a launch, a review-bomb and a balance controversy, testing whether complaint themes give early warning of a score collapse — and finding they don't.
projects.targetIndustryRole: Gaming / community and live-ops teams monitoring launch sentiment
projects.summaryImpact:
**The question was whether complaint themes lead the review score.** If crash complaints spike three days before the score moves, a community team has a usable early-warning signal. I tested it on HELLDIVERS 2 — 886,850 Steam reviews across 271 days covering the launch, the PSN account-linking review-bomb, and the August balance controversy.

**They don't lead.** Both sentiment collapses were triggered by dated developer actions, so complaints and the score moved on the same day. On 2024-05-02 the game sat at 86.7% positive on 968 reviews; the next day Sony announced PSN account linking and the day carried 36,055 reviews at 62.8%, with Sony/PSN complaints going from 21% to 57%. You cannot get early warning of an announcement from reactions to it.

**What the data does support is same-day diagnosis.** The theme mix names the cause within hours, in both directions — Sony/PSN up in May while balance complaints fell; balance 0% to 46% in August while Sony/PSN stayed flat. That is a real operational tool, just not the one I set out to build.
projects.problemSpace:
When a live game's review score falls, the community team's first two questions are what is this about and did we miss a warning sign. The second question is the valuable one: a theme that reliably spikes before the aggregate moves would let a team get ahead of a story instead of reacting to it.

HELLDIVERS 2 is a good test case because it launched well and soured later, which leaves a genuine positive baseline to measure a change against. A game that launched badly gives you nothing to compare to. It also contains two structurally different events: a policy announcement that triggered one of the largest review-bombs in Steam's history, and a balance patch that produced a deeper sentiment trough at a fiftieth of the volume.

stakeholders.description: Needs to know what a spike is about before writing a response, and whether it is still getting worse.
Needs to separate a policy problem from a balance problem from a stability problem, because the fixes sit with different teams.
Wants an early-warning metric. The honest answer here is that review text cannot provide one.

inputs.description: Every public Steam review for HELLDIVERS 2 between 2024-02-08 and 2024-11-04 — 886,850 of them, pulled from Valve's public appreviews endpoint. No API key, no sampling. Sentiment is Steam's own thumbs-up flag rather than a text model, for reasons in Execution.

stats.label: official patches, from the developer's own announcements

dataQuality.label: What the corpus is and isn't
items: **Self-selected.** Steam reviewers are people moved enough to write, not players. Both events here were the kind that motivate writing.
**The thumbs-up is binary.** Of 200 hand-labelled reviews, 19 were genuinely mixed — 'great game, terrible servers' counts identically to 'perfect'. Ambivalence is understated throughout.

**Theme analysis is English-only**, dropping roughly a quarter of the corpus. The largest excluded group is Simplified Chinese, whose complaints may differ on exactly the regional-access issue one event was about.

**Reddit was never pulled** — a scope decision, not a coverage finding. It also removes the likeliest place a lead could have appeared, since complaints usually surface in discussion before they surface as reviews.

closingNote.label: Coverage was verified, not assumed
items: Every chunk of the pull is checked against Steam's own count for that date range and retried if short. Final coverage 100.0%, zero duplicate IDs, zero out-of-window items.
This check exists because the first version did not have it — see Discovery.

surprisingPatterns.label: Surprising Pattern
items: **The review-bomb week was the least duplicated week in the corpus** — 20.7% repeated text against a 28-30% baseline. I expected mass-pasted copypasta to inflate it. Instead the most-repeated texts were positive community memes ('for democracy', 11,851 times), and the only clearly coordinated negative repeats were 'sony' and 'psn' at 0.8% of the week. The collapse was overwhelmingly people writing their own words.

**The famous event was not the deepest one.** The PSN review-bomb produced 76,741 reviews in a day. The August balance patch produced a lower positive share (53.7% on 2024-08-07) at roughly a fiftieth of the volume. Loudest and worst are different measurements.

hypothesisVsReality.label: Hypothesis vs. Reality
items: **Expected:** complaint themes rise days before the aggregate score moves. **Found:** nothing leads. Raw cross-correlation suggested leads in seven of eight themes, up to 12 days — all of it dissolved under three robustness checks.

**Expected:** a sentiment model would be needed to read the reviews. **Found:** two standard models both scored worse than guessing the majority class, and Steam's own thumbs-up flag matched my hand labels far better than either.

**Expected:** review-bomb copypasta would distort the picture and need down-weighting. **Found:** collapsing every repeated text to a single vote changes the headline gap by 0.7 percentage points. The decision did not matter.

deadEnds.label: What didn't work
items: **The first full pull returned 65,496 of 858,566 reviews — 7.6% — with no error.** Steam's cursor pagination stops serving at around 650 pages on a wide date range and simply ends. February through April were missing entirely. Fixed by bisecting the window on Steam's own review counts until every chunk paginates shallowly.

**My integrity check passed that truncated pull.** Duplicate IDs, window bounds, empty text, timestamp gaps — all clean, because every review collected *was* genuine. There were just 92% too few. A validation that only inspects the rows present cannot detect the rows absent, and comparing against an independent total is now the first check rather than an afterthought.

**The cache faithfully preserved the bug.** A bad response was written to disk like any other, so re-running replayed the truncation exactly. Retries had to be made to bypass the cache before they did anything.

**The six-month window truncated the one event worth testing.** The August controversy began three days before the window closed. I extended to 271 days, because a null measured on a truncated event is an artefact of the window rather than a result.

executionDeadEnds.label: The result I nearly published
items: Raw cross-correlation produced a clean-looking table showing a 12-day lead for developer-conduct complaints. It was noise. Reporting the best of 29 lags means taking the extreme of 29 attempts, and chance alone produces a median best-of-29-lags correlation of about −0.15 — most of what the table showed.

A rotation test, a correction for testing eight themes, and a sensitivity check on how thin a day is allowed to be each removed it independently. The apparent leads moved from +3 to +12 to −8 days as measurement improved, which is what noise does and a real signal does not.

methodology.heading: Pull, verified against an independent count
methodology.description: Cursor-paginated pull of Valve's public appreviews endpoint, chunked by bisecting on Steam's own review counts so no single query paginates deep enough to truncate. Every page cached by (appid, cursor, date range); every chunk checked against the expected count and retried with the cache bypassed if short.

methodology.heading: Sentiment: Steam's flag, after rejecting two models
methodology.description: I hand-labelled 200 reviews blind and tested both scorers against them. **VADER agreed 61.5%, a RoBERTa sentiment model 64.0% — against a 72.0% majority-class baseline.** Both did worse than always guessing 'positive'. The failure is specific: this game's players express enthusiasm through violence and self-deprecation ('I got hit by an explosion, shot into the air, then stomped by a robot 10/10'), which general-purpose models read as negative. Steam's own thumbs-up matched my labels 95.0%, so the index uses that and the models stay in the repo as the evidence for the decision.

methodology.heading: Themes: a keyword taxonomy, seeded from the data
methodology.description: Nine themes, 182 seed phrases, mined by measuring which terms are distinctive of thumbs-down reviews rather than guessed. Matching is word-boundary substring — transparent and explainable line by line, which a learned classifier would not be. Multi-label, because 'nerfed into the ground and it crashes' is genuinely two complaints. Coverage 69.6%; the remainder is partly missing vocabulary and partly complaint with no complaint words in it.

methodology.heading: The lag test, and why composition not volume
methodology.description: Themes are measured as a share of each day's negatives, not as raw counts. Volume and the aggregate score are both functions of how many people were angry that day, so correlating them recovers a relationship that exists by construction. Both series are differenced before correlating, because levels are dominated by one enormous event.

methodology.heading: Three checks before believing the result
methodology.description: A rotation-based permutation test built for the statistic actually reported (best of 29 lags); a Bonferroni correction for testing eight themes; and a sensitivity sweep on minimum day size. A test in the suite plants a three-day lead in synthetic data and asserts the method recovers it — reporting a null is only honest if the method could have found a signal.

methodology.heading: The threshold, derived rather than asserted
methodology.description: Candidate alert rules were tested against the data. A level rule ('below 72% positive') fires on 35 of 271 days, 29 of them nothing. A 12-point single-day drop fires three times in nine months — 3 May, 6 and 7 August — with no false alarms. At 10 points it adds four non-events; at 20 it misses August entirely.

keyResults.label: Key Results
items: **No theme leads the score.** Only Sony/PSN complaints correlate with it at all (r = −0.30), and the best lag is zero. Every apparent lead failed at least one of three robustness checks.
**Same-day diagnosis works.** On 2024-05-03 Sony/PSN complaints went 21% to 57% while balance complaints fell; on 2024-08-06 balance went 0% to 46% while Sony/PSN stayed at 3%.
**A change-based alert beats a level-based one decisively.** 3 alerts with zero false positives, against 35 alerts with 29 false positives for the obvious threshold.
**Recovery is as visible as collapse.** 2024-05-06 — the day Sony reversed — was the busiest day in the corpus at 78,185 reviews and 88.3% positive, up from 67.9% the day before.

projects.businessInterpretation:
For a community team, this is an instrumentation tool rather than a forecast. It will not tell you a storm is coming, because in both of these cases the storm was the studio's own announcement on a date it chose. What it will do is answer 'what is this about' within hours of a score moving, without anyone reading a review — and it distinguishes a policy problem from a balance problem from a stability problem, which matters because those fixes sit with three different teams.

The alerting recommendation is the practical output: watch the day-over-day change, not the level. A level threshold fires on a quarter of the calendar and a team learns to ignore it inside a fortnight. If genuine early warning is the goal, it needs data that moves before the announcement — crash telemetry, refund rates, or discussion-thread volume — none of which lives in review text.

items.text: Alert on a 12-point single-day fall in positive share, not on the level. When it trips, read the theme mix before reading reviews — it named the cause correctly in both events here, within hours.
Expect no warning from review text for announcement-driven events. The gap between a decision landing and sentiment moving was under 24 hours both times.

The headline here is a null, and the interesting work is in what it took to trust it: a truncated pull that looked clean, an integrity check that passed it, and a 12-day 'lead' that three independent checks dissolved.

limitations: Steam reviewers self-select — this measures people moved enough to write, not players.
Sentiment is Steam's binary thumbs-up. 19 of 200 hand-labelled reviews were genuinely mixed and the flag cannot represent them, so ambivalence is understated throughout.

Theme matching is keyword-based at 69.6% coverage. Some of the remainder is unreachable by any keyword list — 'Arrowhead struck gold but are determined to find copper' is a complaint with no complaint vocabulary in it.
Theme analysis is English-only, excluding roughly a quarter of the corpus — most notably Simplified Chinese reviews, on a project where one of the two events was about regional access.
Two events in one game. The mechanism (announcement-driven events cannot be predicted from reactions) should generalise; the specific thresholds should not be assumed to.
nextSteps: Test the same method on a launch whose sentiment decayed gradually rather than breaking on an announcement — that is where a lead could plausibly exist.
Add discussion-forum or Reddit volume as a second source, since complaints usually surface there before they surface as reviews.
Topic modelling as a cross-check on the ~30% of complaints no keyword reaches.
